title: Boyle's law: variation of volume with pressure at constant temperature
objective: To study how the volume of a fixed mass of air varies with pressure at constant temperature.
To plot graphs of P against V and of P against 1/V.
To verify that PV is constant.

theory.statement: Boyle's law states that at constant temperature the volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure. Equivalently, the product of pressure and volume is a constant.
theory.derivationNote: The apparatus traps a fixed mass of dry air in the closed limb of a U-tube above a mercury thread. The pressure of the trapped air is the atmospheric pressure plus the difference in the mercury levels: raising the open limb increases the pressure and compresses the air, while lowering it does the reverse. Because the tube is of uniform bore, the volume of the trapped air is proportional to the length of the air column, so that length may be used directly in place of the volume. Boyle's law predicts PV = constant, so P = k(1/V). A graph of P against V is a rectangular hyperbola, which is difficult to test by eye. A graph of P against 1/V, however, is a straight line passing through the origin, and its slope equals the constant PV. This is why the second graph is the real test of the law. Kinetic theory explains the result: reducing the volume increases the number of molecules per unit volume, so more collisions occur with each unit area of wall each second and the pressure rises in proportion.
keyEquations: P = k × (1/V), so P against 1/V is a straight line of slope k
Pressure of trapped air = atmospheric pressure + difference in mercury levels
Volume ∝ length of the air column, for a tube of uniform bore

apparatus.name: Boyle's law apparatus
apparatus.spec: closed and open limbs of uniform bore joined at the base
apparatus.why: Traps a fixed mass of air whose pressure can be varied by moving the mercury

apparatus.name: Mercury
apparatus.why: Its high density gives a large pressure change over a manageable height, and it does not wet the glass

apparatus.name: Metre scales
apparatus.spec: two, fixed beside each limb, least count 0.1 cm
apparatus.why: Read the mercury levels in both limbs and the length of the air column

apparatus.name: Fortin's barometer
apparatus.why: Gives the atmospheric pressure on the day, which is added to the level difference

apparatus.name: Thermometer
apparatus.why: Confirms that the temperature stays constant throughout

apparatus.name: Levelling screws and plumb line
apparatus.why: Ensure the tubes are vertical, so the level difference is a true vertical height

procedure.text: Check with the plumb line that both limbs are vertical, and read the barometer to obtain the atmospheric pressure.
Note the temperature of the room. It must stay constant for the whole experiment.
Adjust the open limb until the mercury stands at the same level in both limbs. The trapped air is then at exactly atmospheric pressure.
Measure the length of the trapped air column and record it with the corresponding pressure.
Raise the open limb slowly so that the mercury rises and the air is compressed. Wait a minute for the temperature to settle before reading.
Record the new level difference and the new length of the air column.
Repeat for at least six different positions, some with the open limb raised and some with it lowered.
For each reading calculate the pressure, the volume and their product. Check whether the product is constant.
Plot P against V, which gives a curve, and then P against 1/V, which should give a straight line through the origin.

steps: Pressure of trapped air P = atmospheric pressure + level difference
Volume V = length of air column × area of bore
Compute the product P × V for every reading
Plot P against 1/V; the slope of the line is the constant PV
Check that the line passes through the origin

secondary.quantity: Spread of PV across all readings

expectedResult.statement: The product of pressure and volume is the same for every reading within experimental error. The P against V graph is a hyperbola, while the P against 1/V graph is a straight line passing through the origin whose slope equals the constant PV. Boyle's law is verified.

safety: Mercury and its vapour are toxic. Never touch mercury with bare hands and never leave the apparatus open.
Report any spillage at once; scattered droplets must be collected by the teacher, not swept up.
Work in a well ventilated room and wash your hands thoroughly afterwards.
Raise and lower the limb slowly. A sudden movement can force mercury out of the open end.
Do not warm any part of the apparatus, both because mercury vapour pressure rises and because the experiment requires constant temperature.
sourcesOfError: Compressing the gas quickly warms it, so the process is not isothermal and the reading drifts.
The bore of the tube may not be perfectly uniform, so length is not exactly proportional to volume.
Air dissolved in or trapped beneath the mercury alters the mass of gas being studied.
Parallax while reading the mercury levels against the scales.
The tubes not being exactly vertical, so the measured level difference is not the true vertical height.
Change of room temperature during the experiment.

viva.question: State Boyle's law.
viva.expectedConcept: At constant temperature, the volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, so that PV is constant.
viva.answerLogic: Must include both the fixed mass and the constant temperature conditions.

viva.question: Why is a graph of P against 1/V plotted as well as P against V?
viva.expectedConcept: The P against V graph is a hyperbola, and it is very hard to judge by eye whether a curve is a true hyperbola or merely some other decreasing curve. Plotting P against 1/V converts the relationship into a straight line through the origin, which can be tested at a glance and whose slope gives the constant.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the second graph is just a repetition of the first.

viva.question: How is the pressure of the trapped air found?
viva.expectedConcept: It equals the atmospheric pressure plus the difference in the mercury levels. If the level in the open limb is higher, the difference is added; if lower, it is subtracted.
viva.answerLogic: P = P₀ ± Δh with the correct sign.
viva.commonMisconception: Taking the level difference alone as the pressure and forgetting the atmosphere.

viva.question: Why may the length of the air column be used instead of its volume?
viva.expectedConcept: The tube is of uniform bore, so the volume is the length multiplied by a constant area of cross-section. Since a constant factor cancels from both sides of PV = constant, the length may be used directly.
viva.answerLogic: Volume proportional to length for uniform bore.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing the area must be measured.

viva.question: Explain Boyle's law from kinetic theory.
viva.expectedConcept: Pressure arises from molecular collisions with the walls. Reducing the volume at constant temperature packs the same number of molecules into a smaller space without changing their average speed, so collisions with each unit area of wall occur more frequently and the pressure rises in inverse proportion to the volume.
viva.answerLogic: Collision frequency per unit area scales as number density.
viva.commonMisconception: Saying the molecules move faster when compressed, which would mean a temperature change.

viva.question: What happens if the gas is compressed quickly?
viva.expectedConcept: Work is done on the gas and it warms, so the process is adiabatic rather than isothermal. Boyle's law does not then apply, and the volume reading drifts as the gas cools back to room temperature. The limb must be moved slowly and time allowed before each reading.
viva.answerLogic: Adiabatic compression breaks the constant-temperature condition.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming speed of operation cannot affect the result.

viva.question: Why is mercury used rather than water?
viva.expectedConcept: Mercury is about 13.6 times as dense as water, so a given pressure change needs a column only a fraction as tall and the apparatus stays a manageable size. Mercury also does not wet glass, gives a clean well-defined meniscus, and does not evaporate appreciably into the trapped gas.

viva.question: Does Boyle's law hold at very high pressures?
viva.expectedConcept: No. At high pressure the molecules are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container and the intermolecular forces become significant. The gas then departs from ideal behaviour and PV is no longer constant.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating Boyle's law as exact under all conditions.

viva.question: The product PV in your table varies by two per cent. Has the law failed?
viva.expectedConcept: No. Two per cent is comparable with the combined uncertainty in reading the mercury levels and the air column to 0.1 cm. The law is verified if the scatter in PV is no larger than the experimental error.
viva.answerLogic: Compare scatter with the estimated uncertainty.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting the product to be identical to every decimal place.

viva.question: A bubble rises from the bottom of a lake. What happens to its volume?
viva.expectedConcept: It expands. As the bubble rises the pressure of the water above it falls, and by Boyle's law the volume increases in inverse proportion, assuming the temperature is roughly constant. This is why divers are told never to hold their breath while ascending.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the bubble shrinks under the weight of water above.

preLab.question: According to Boyle's law, if the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is doubled at constant temperature, its volume:
preLab.feedback: PV is constant, so doubling P must halve V.

preLab.question: A graph of pressure against volume for a gas at constant temperature is:
options: A straight line through the origin
preLab.feedback: PV = constant is the equation of a rectangular hyperbola. Plotting P against 1/V straightens it.

preLab.question: The pressure of the trapped air equals:
options: Atmospheric pressure plus or minus the level difference
Atmospheric pressure divided by the level difference
preLab.feedback: The mercury column adds to or subtracts from the atmospheric pressure depending on which limb stands higher.

duringLab.question: Record at least five different pressures.
Keep the temperature constant throughout the run.

postLab.question: State the mean value of the product P × V from your table.
postLab.feedback: For the sample used, PV comes out at about 1140 cm Hg · cm³ at every pressure.

postLab.question: Your P against 1/V graph is a straight line through the origin. This shows that:
options: P is inversely proportional to V
P does not depend on V
postLab.feedback: A straight line through the origin when plotted against 1/V means P ∝ 1/V, which is Boyle's law.

postLab.question: You raised the open limb quickly and the reading kept drifting. This is because:
options: The gas was warmed by the compression and is cooling again
postLab.feedback: Rapid compression does work on the gas and warms it. Boyle's law needs constant temperature, so the limb must be moved slowly and time allowed before reading.

scientificValidation.formula: PV = constant; P = k(1/V); P = P₀ ± Δh
assumptions: Temperature of the trapped air stays constant
Tube of uniform bore, so volume is proportional to column length
The trapped air behaves as an ideal gas over this range
No air leaks past the mercury
Atmospheric pressure is steady during the experiment
scientificValidation.validRange: Level difference −40 to +40 cm; total pressure 36 to 116 cm of mercury
scientificValidation.unitSystem: Pressure in cm of mercury, volume in cm³
edgeCases: A P-V graph is a hyperbola and fits a straight line badly; P against 1/V fits well
Quick compression is adiabatic, not isothermal — warned
Readings clustered near atmospheric pressure give no useful spread — warned
A near-zero pressure would break the mercury thread — blocked
expectedBehaviour: The product PV is the same for every reading to within 4%
Halving the volume doubles the pressure
P against 1/V is straight with r² above 0.998 and passes through the origin
The slope of that line equals the constant PV
